facts.statement: Diademodus lived during the Late Devonian Period.
facts.quote: Diademodus is an extinct genus of phoebodontid elasmobranch that lived during the Late Devonian Period.

facts.statement: Diademodus was a long, slender cartilaginous fish reaching up to 40 cm in body length.
facts.quote: According to Harris, Diademodus was a long, slender cartilaginous fish that reached a body length of up to 40 cm.

facts.statement: The body of Diademodus was covered in tooth-like dermal denticles.
facts.quote: Like most cartilaginous fishes, its body was covered in tooth-like dermal denticles.

facts.statement: The pectoral fins of Diademodus were positioned approximately 14 cm from the tip of the head.
facts.quote: Its pectoral fins were positioned unusually far back along the body, approximately 14 cm from the tip of the head.

facts.statement: The pectoral fins of Diademodus extended only 5.2 cm along the body and projected about 2.5 cm outward.
facts.quote: They were also extremely small, extending only 5.2 cm along the body and projecting about 2.5 cm outward.

facts.statement: Individual teeth of Diademodus bore between nine and seventeen cusps depending on the species.
facts.quote: Individual teeth bore between nine and seventeen cusps in total, depending on the species.

facts.statement: Diademodus was originally classified in the family Coronodontidae, which included only the genera Coronodus and Diademodus.
facts.quote: Diademodus was originally classified within the family Coronodontidae, a group that included only the genera Coronodus and Diademodus.

facts.statement: John E. Harris proposed that Diademodus had a scavenging lifestyle based on its small teeth.
facts.quote: Harris proposed that its small teeth indicated a scavenging lifestyle.

facts.statement: Harris suggested Diademodus hydei was piscivorous because bony fish scales were found in the stomach region of a fossil.
facts.quote: He also suggested that D. hydei was piscivorous, as bony fish scales belonging to palaeoniscoids are preserved in the stomach region of the fossil.

facts.statement: Michał Ginter suggested in 2008 that Diademodus utahensis may have had weakly attached teeth, limiting its ability to capture large prey.
facts.quote: In the 2008 description of D. utahensis, paleontologist Michał Ginter suggested that the teeth of this species may have been weakly attached to the jaws, potentially limiting the animal's ability to capture large prey.

facts.statement: Teeth attributable to Diademodus have been found in Utah, Nevada, Western Australia, and Russia.
facts.quote: Teeth attributable to this genus have also been reported from Utah, Nevada, Western Australia, and Russia.

rejected.statement: Diademodus was first described by John E. Harris in 1951 based on a body fossil found in the Cleveland Shale formation of Ohio.
rejected.quote: The genus was first described by paleontologist John E. Harris on the basis of a body fossil from the Cleveland Shale formation of Ohio.
